Run-up settings Past run-up = buying 10 trading days before each ex-date and selling the last day before it. Past green-dot trades = buying at the first green dot 3-14 days out and selling the last day before the ex-date. The green dot is worked out from daily prices with the WaveTrend rule Cipher B uses (cross up while oversold); always confirm it on the chart with the MC-B link. Sell by the date shown to keep the run-up and not receive the dividend.

How to use: buy on or before Buy by (the last trading day before the ex-date, allowing for holidays); you may sell from the Ex-date and keep the dividend. Rows marked est. are projected from last year's schedule and are not announced yet; confirm before buying. Income on capital (in the tax table) uses your capital in each stock's own currency (pence prices are converted) and your tax rate: cash after withholding, then an after-tax estimate per payment and per year, with the foreign tax offset applied and ASX franking credits added. Company or super fund? Change the tax rate. Rating (0-100) = yield 25 (franked yield for ASX) + past ex-day capture 25 + payment record 10 + regularity 10 + growth 10 + liquidity 10 + tax efficiency 10. Hover a rating for the parts. Partnerships taxed at about 47% are capped at 40. It is a rules-based score, not a recommendation. Dividend run-up mode (button at the top) switches the page to the run-up strategy: buy 1-2 weeks before the ex-date when the daily green dot appears, then sell by the Sell by date, before the ex-date, so you keep the price run-up and do not receive the dividend. The green dot is calculated from daily prices using the WaveTrend cross-up-while-oversold rule that Cipher B uses; confirm it on the chart with the MC-B link because chart settings can differ. Past run-up and past green-dot trades show what this plan would have returned around each stock's previous dividends: they are history, not a forecast, and exclude brokerage and tax. Liquidity = average daily traded value (3-month average volume x price) converted to AUD at approximate exchange rates: green A$25M+ a day (high), amber A$3M-25M (medium), red under A$3M (low). Thin liquidity means wider spreads and harder exits around the ex-date. Past ex-day result = what buying the close before and selling at the ex-date close would have returned over the last dividends (price move plus dividend), with the wins. Prices usually fall by about the dividend, so many show about 0% or less. Paid shows the announced pay date where Yahoo has it; otherwise it is estimated (marked ~) from the stock's last known gap or the market's usual gap between ex-date and payment. IB ✓ / IB ? is an exchange-level check only (✓ = Interactive Brokers offers that exchange; ? = newly added or restricted by region or account, e.g. Korea, Brazil, South Africa, Mexico, India, Taiwan): confirm each symbol and your trading permissions inside IBKR. Franking uses the percentages in the script (verify on the announcement); the credit is 30/70 of the cash dividend x franking %. Hold 45 days (see the date) to claim it; the small-holder exemption covers credits up to $5,000 a year. Options that cut your risk (puts, deep ITM calls) can stop days counting, and the ATO treats some dividend-stripping arrangements as tax avoidance, so get advice. Tax table: rates are what an Australian resident with treaty paperwork normally sees. Rows marked Checked were confirmed against official or primary sources; others are standard treaty rates to confirm with your broker. Foreign tax is claimed as a foreign income tax offset (simple method up to $1,000). General information only, not tax or financial advice. Liquid options only keeps stocks where the script found reasonably tradable options (a bid, a spread of up to about 30% of the price, and some open interest or volume); every stock is checked once a week (saved in options_cache.json), whether or not its ex-date is confirmed. Stocks Yahoo has no options for, which includes most non-US markets, are hidden by this box. Options: Put = ~5% out-of-the-money put expiring after the ex-date; Net = dividend % minus put cost. ITM call = short-dated in-the-money call; strike chosen so time value is at least 1.25x the dividend. Locked = return if called away (before costs); BE = breakeven. 100 shares per contract, liquid contracts only. Yahoo ex-dates can be projected, so confirm with the company. Brokerage is not included.

Distribution schedule (QQQI pays monthly)

Ex-dividend datePay dateAmount per shareAnnualised yield at today's priceStatus
How this page works: you buy QQQI with your capital plus the loan, sell one call per 100 shares at a strike below the price (in the money), collect the premium now, collect the monthly distribution if you still hold the shares on the ex-dividend date, and pay loan interest. Return if called = (time value + distributions) / QQQI price, where time value = premium minus the part of the premium that is just the in-the-money amount (intrinsic value). If QQQI finishes above the strike the shares are sold at the strike, so that is the most you can make on those shares. Cushion = how far QQQI can fall from today before the trade loses money (premium plus distributions received). Early-assignment risk: a call that is in the money can be exercised the day before the ex-dividend date by a buyer who wants the distribution. That happens when the call's remaining time value on that day is less than the distribution. Time value shrinks as expiry nears, so the page scales today's time value down to the day before the ex-date (calls expiring just after the ex-date are usually HIGH). If it happens you keep the premium but lose that month's distribution, so the page counts the distribution only for calls rated LOW or MEDIUM. Close or roll such a call before the ex-date if you want to keep the distribution. Suggestions only use options that pass your open-interest and spread limits: Highest income = best annualised return; Balanced = best annualised return with at least 3% cushion; Most protection = biggest cushion while earning at least 60% of the best return; Keep the distribution = best option rated LOW or MEDIUM risk. Option prices come from Yahoo (about 15 minutes delayed) and bid/ask are often blank when the US market is closed (about 1:30am-8am Victoria time at the moment), so run the script while it is open, and always check the live price in your broker before placing the order. The loan rate, margin and expected dividend are your assumptions. Writing options needs options approval with your broker. This is a planning tool, not financial or tax advice; past distributions do not guarantee future ones, and QQQI can fall in value.
